title: T1566.002 — Phishing - Spearphishing Link
subtitle: Watch the attack unfold.
aria: Animated diagram of a spearphishing link attack: the attacker registers a fake domain, sends an email with a link, the victim clicks it and logs in on a fake page, and the attacker replays the stolen session cookie against the company identity provider. A full written description of every step follows below the canvas.

nodes.label: Attacker
nodes.tip: The threat actor. They build the fake site, send the email, and later reuse what they steal.

nodes.label: Email Gateway
nodes.tip: The company mail security service. It checks sender identity, attachments, and URLs before delivery.

nodes.label: User Mailbox
nodes.tip: The targeted employee's mailbox, hosted in the company mail service.

nodes.label: User Browser
nodes.tip: The victim's web browser. Every click, DNS query, and page load can leave telemetry here.

nodes.label: Phishing Site
nodes.tip: The attacker's fake login page. It proxies the real portal so the victim sees a genuine site while the attacker records credentials and cookies.

nodes.label: Corporate IdP
nodes.tip: The identity provider (for example Entra ID or Okta). It issues sessions and logs every sign-in.

nodes.label: SOC / Defender
nodes.tip: The security operations center. It collects logs from mail, network, endpoint, and identity sources.

steps.title: Stage the infrastructure
steps.caption: the attacker registers the look-alike domain sso-login-portal-example[.]com, obtains a TLS certificate, and installs an AiTM phishing kit that copies the real login page.
steps.defender: Monitor Certificate Transparency logs and newly-registered-domain (NRD) feeds. Domains that look like your brand and get a certificate on the same day deserve a look before any mail arrives.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Send the link
steps.caption: the attacker emails the victim a short, urgent message with one link and no attachment. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass, so the gateway delivers it.
steps.defender: Do not treat DMARC as a phishing verdict. Alert on messages with zero attachments plus one unclassified URL, especially when the display name matches your IT or HR department.

steps.title: The victim clicks
steps.caption: the browser follows a redirect and resolves the fresh domain. DNS and proxy logs capture the query, but the uncategorized domain is allowed.
steps.defender: Log all DNS and proxy traffic per user. An uncategorized or newly-registered domain hit from a corporate device is worth an alert even before anything bad is confirmed.

steps.title: The fake page loads
steps.caption: the kit reverse-proxies the real sign-in portal, so the victim sees a pixel-perfect login page. The only visible clues are a 3-day-old certificate and a known kit fingerprint.
steps.defender: Fingerprint AiTM kits on the proxy: look for kit-specific paths, resource hashes, or TLS certificates younger than 7 days on login-style pages.

detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Credentials and MFA are captured
steps.caption: the victim types the password and approves the push. The kit forwards everything to the real portal in real time and steals the resulting session cookie.
steps.defender: There is no identity alert at this moment. This is why detection must start earlier, at DNS, proxy, and mail layers, and why phishing-resistant MFA matters.

steps.title: Session cookie replay
steps.caption: the attacker imports the stolen cookie on their own infrastructure and opens the mailbox. The IdP sees a successful non-interactive sign-in from a new device and network, with no password event before it.
steps.defender: Your best identity signal: a successful sign-in with no corresponding password authentication, new ASN, and a new device fingerprint. Correlate it with the earlier proxy hit on the phishing domain.

detection.label: Partial signal
detection.detail: A weak signal exists but is not yet a confirmed alert.

steps.title: Access and persistence
steps.caption: the attacker reads the mailbox, searches for financial threads, and creates a hidden forwarding rule to keep a copy of every future message.
steps.defender: Alert on new inbox forwarding rules, especially forwarding to external domains, and on mailbox permission changes that follow a suspicious sign-in.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Defender responds
steps.caption: the SOC correlates the proxy hit, the passwordless sign-in, and the forwarding rule, then disables the account, revokes every session and token, and blocks the phishing domain everywhere.
steps.defender: Turning a breach into a catch: password reset alone is not enough, because the stolen cookie survives it. Revoke sessions and refresh tokens, and build the detections you were missing.
